blocks.md: Total inequality can be split into two parts. Within-group inequality is how much people who look alike — same education, same experience — still differ in pay. Between-group inequality is how much the averages of different groups differ, like the gap between graduates and non-graduates. Some measures split exactly into these two parts; others do not. Knowing which part is driving a change tells you very different stories about the labor market.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: Policy and research questions usually hinge on whether rising inequality comes from gaps between groups or from widening differences inside them.
Total inequality across a population splits into two sources: dispersion **within** groups and differences **between** group averages.

- **Within-group**: workers with the same observable characteristics (education, experience, gender) still earn different amounts. Often called *residual* inequality, because it is what is left after conditioning on observables.
- **Between-group**: differences in average outcomes across groups — the [Skill Premium](note:skill-premium), the gender gap, the racial gap. Usually measured with a [Log Wage Gap](note:log-wage-gap).
Only some measures split cleanly. The [Variance of Log Income](note:variance-of-log-income) does, by the [Law of Total Variance](note:law-of-total-variance):

blocks.tex: \underbrace{\mathrm{Var}(\ln y)}_{\text{total}} = \underbrace{\sum_g s_g\,\mathrm{Var}(\ln y \mid g)}_{\text{within}} + \underbrace{\sum_g s_g\,\big(\overline{\ln y}_g - \overline{\ln y}\big)^2}_{\text{between}}

blocks.md: **Worked example** (nine-worker data from [Defining Inequality](note:defining-inequality), grouped by education): total $\mathrm{Var}(\ln w) = 0.0857$, of which within = 0.0820 and between = 0.0037. About 96% of inequality in this toy data is within education groups.
The [Gini Coefficient](note:gini-coefficient) does **not** decompose this way unless group income ranges do not overlap — there is a residual overlap term.

The [Shift-Share Decomposition](note:shift-share-decomposition) uses the same logic on wage-bill shares: changes *between* industries vs changes *within* industries. Same word, different object — be precise about what is being decomposed.

A regression of $\ln w$ on group dummies estimates the between-group component directly: coefficients are differences in group means ([Indicator Variables](note:indicator-variables)). The residual variance is the within-group component.

sections.heading: Why the two can move together: unobserved skill

blocks.md: Between- and within-group inequality need not move together — but they do when the observed groups are a **noisy measure of the skill that is actually paid**. Suppose wages depend only on unobserved ability ($w_h$ or $w_\ell$), and education is correlated with ability: a share $a_C$ of college workers and a smaller share $a_N$ of non-college workers are high ability. The college premium is a ratio of mixtures:
In logs the same model gives a between-group gap of $(a_C - a_N)\ln\zeta$ and a within-group variance of $a_g(1 - a_g)(\ln\zeta)^2$ in group $g$: **both** grow with the ability premium.
**Worked example** ($a_C = 0.6$, $a_N = 0.2$, ability premium rising from 2 to 3):

| | $\zeta = 2$ | $\zeta = 3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| College premium $\kappa$ (ratio of means) | 1.333 | 1.571 |
| Log gap between groups | 0.277 | 0.439 |
| Within-group variance of log wages, college | 0.115 | 0.290 |
| Within-group variance of log wages, non-college | 0.077 | 0.193 |

If education measured ability perfectly ($a_C = 1$, $a_N = 0$), within-group variance would be zero and all inequality would be between groups. The co-movement comes from the *measurement error* in the grouping — and it is an assumption, not a law: other forces (composition, institutions, noise in wages) can move the two parts in opposite directions.

sections.heading: The within share depends on the groups

blocks.md: Splitting groups more finely can only move variance from the within part to the between part (the between part of a finer partition is never smaller). A claim like "two-thirds of inequality is within groups" is always relative to the characteristics used to form the cells.

Random reporting error in wages leaves group means unchanged but adds its variance to every group's dispersion, so it inflates the within part one-for-one — see [Classical Measurement Error](note:classical-measurement-error). Survey [Top Coding](note:top-coding) works the other way, compressing the top of high-wage groups.
